22.why: A media streaming server needs maximum read speed and capacity. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 0 (RAID-0) stripes data across disks for performance, and the media can be re-created if a disk fails.

whyNot.B: Mirroring halves usable capacity and adds redundancy that a streaming workload does not need as much as speed.
whyNot.C: Striping with single parity adds write overhead and capacity cost that a speed-focused streaming server does not need.
whyNot.D: Striping with double parity has the highest write overhead and capacity cost, which is unnecessary for replaceable media.

23.why: An authentication server needs high availability and simple, fast recovery. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 1 (RAID-1) mirrors data to a second disk, so one disk can fail without downtime or data loss.

whyNot.A: Striping with no redundancy means one disk failure destroys all authentication data and takes the server down.
whyNot.C: Single parity striping needs at least three disks and has slower writes, which is not the expected match for a small authentication server.
whyNot.D: Double parity striping needs at least four disks and has heavy write overhead, which is more than an authentication server's profile calls for.

24.why: An email archive is read often and written less often, and it needs capacity efficiency with fault tolerance. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 5 (RAID-5) stripes data with distributed single parity and survives one disk failure.

whyNot.A: Striping with no parity gives no fault tolerance, so one disk failure would lose the archive.
whyNot.B: Mirroring survives a disk failure but wastes half the capacity, which is costly for a large archive.
whyNot.D: Striping with double parity survives two failures but costs more capacity and write speed than an archive requires.

25.why: An identity management server holds critical data and warrants the strongest protection. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 6 (RAID-6) uses double distributed parity and survives two simultaneous disk failures.

whyNot.A: Striping with no parity provides no fault tolerance for critical identity data.
whyNot.B: Mirroring tolerates only one disk failure in a pair, which is less resilient than double parity.
whyNot.C: Single parity striping survives only one disk failure, so it is less protective than double parity for critical identity data.

26.why: Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 5 (RAID-5) on four disks stripes data across all of them with distributed parity, giving the capacity of three data disks and one disk's worth of parity.

whyNot.B: Mirroring with no parity describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 1 (RAID-1), not level 5.
whyNot.C: Two parity boxes describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 6 (RAID-6), and four data stripes would leave no room for parity.
whyNot.D: Two data stripes with no parity describes striping without redundancy and does not match level 5 on four disks.

27.why: Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 6 (RAID-6) uses two parity blocks. On four disks, the parity boxes are checked and the array tolerates two disk failures.

whyNot.A: One parity box describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 5 (RAID-5), which tolerates only one disk failure.
whyNot.B: Mirroring with no parity describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 1 (RAID-1), not level 6.
whyNot.D: Two data stripes with no parity gives no fault tolerance, which does not match level 6.

34.why: CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache is the most volatile evidence source because it holds data for nanoseconds and changes constantly, so it is collected first in the order of volatility.

whyNot.C: Swap space lives on disk and survives longer than RAM (Random Access Memory), so it ranks third.
whyNot.D: A hard drive keeps data without power, making it the least volatile of these sources.

35.why: RAM (Random Access Memory) is the second most volatile source: its contents vanish at power loss, but they persist longer than CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache.

whyNot.A: CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache changes faster than RAM (Random Access Memory), so it is first in the order of volatility.
whyNot.C: Swap space is stored on disk and lasts longer than RAM (Random Access Memory), so it ranks third.
whyNot.D: A hard drive retains data without power, so it is the least volatile of these sources.

36.why: Swap space is third because it extends RAM (Random Access Memory) onto disk, so it is less volatile than memory but still temporary and rewritten as the system runs.

whyNot.B: RAM (Random Access Memory) loses data at power loss and changes faster than swap, so it ranks second.

37.why: The hard drive is the least volatile of these sources because it stores data persistently without power, so it is collected last in the order of volatility.

whyNot.C: Swap space is temporary paging data that changes while the system runs, so it ranks third.
